Coprime matchings of divisor sets

Max A. Alekseyev Address: Department of Mathematics, The George Washington University, Washington, DC 20052, USA Email address: maxal@gwu.edu
Abstract.

For a positive integer nn, let D⁡(n)D(n) be its set of positive divisors and put N:=τ⁡(n)=|D⁡(n)|N:=\tau(n)=|D(n)|. We characterize the arithmetic progressions 𝒫\mathcal{P} of length NN that admit a bijection with D⁡(n)D(n) pairing relatively prime integers. Such a coprime matching exists if and only if, for every prime p|np\mid n, at most N/(νp​(n)+1)N/(\nu_{p}(n)+1) terms of 𝒫\mathcal{P} are divisible by pp, where νp​(n)\nu_{p}(n) is the exponent of pp in nn. Call nn an MM-number if pp∤np^{p}\nmid n for every prime pp. We prove that D⁡(n)D(n) can be matched with every primitive arithmetic progression of length NN, meaning one whose first term and common difference are coprime, if and only if nn is an MM-number. This proves a conjecture of McNew and Pomerance. We call nn matchable if D⁡(n)D(n) admits a coprime matching with the primitive arithmetic progression {1,2,…,N}\{1,2,\ldots,N\}. The general criterion implies that nn is matchable if and only if ⌊N/p⌋≤N/(νp​(n)+1)\lfloor N/p\rfloor\leq N/(\nu_{p}(n)+1) for all p|np\mid n. We explicitly classify the matchable non-MM-numbers, settle a conjectured divisor criterion, and prove that every divisor of a matchable integer is matchable. A Vandermonde determinant gives the required matchings under bounds on the prime exponents, while a partition into shorter progressions handles the remaining cases.

Key words and phrases: 
coprime matching, divisor set, arithmetic progression, Vandermonde determinant
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 05C70, 11A25; Secondary 11B25

1. Introduction

Given two finite sets of integers with the same number of elements, a coprime matching between them is a bijection under which corresponding integers are relatively prime. We write [1,N]:={1,2,…,N}[1,N]:=\{1,2,\ldots,N\}.

We study coprime matchings from divisor sets to arithmetic progressions. For a positive integer nn, let

D(n):={d∈ℤ>0:d∣n},τ(n):=|D(n)|.D(n):=\{d\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}:d\mid n\},\qquad\tau(n):=|D(n)|.

We write rad⁡(n):=∏p|np\rad(n):=\prod_{p\mid n}p, where the product ranges over primes, and let νp​(n)\nu_{p}(n) denote the exponent of pp in the prime factorization of nn. We ask when D⁡(n)D(n) admits a coprime matching with a prescribed arithmetic progression of length τ⁡(n)\tau(n). We call an arithmetic progression primitive if its first term and common difference are coprime.

For a prime p|np\mid n, exactly τ⁡(n)/(νp​(n)+1)\tau(n)/(\nu_{p}(n)+1) divisors of nn are not divisible by pp. Every term of the progression divisible by pp must be matched to one of these divisors. Our main result shows that the resulting counting bounds, considered separately for each prime dividing nn, give a complete criterion.

Theorem 1.1 (Arithmetic progression criterion).

Let nn be a positive integer, put N:=τ⁡(n)N:=\tau(n), and let

𝒫:={a+bt:t=0,1,…,N−1},a∈ℤ,b∈ℤ>0.\mathcal{P}:=\{a+bt:t=0,1,\ldots,N-1\},\qquad a\in\mathbb{Z},\quad b\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}.

For each prime p|np\mid n, put

cp(𝒫):=#{x∈𝒫:p∣x}.c_{p}(\mathcal{P}):=\#\{x\in\mathcal{P}:p\mid x\}.

Then D⁡(n)D(n) admits a coprime matching with 𝒫\mathcal{P} if and only if

(1) cp​(𝒫)≤Nνp​(n)+1for every prime ​p|n.c_{p}(\mathcal{P})\leq\frac{N}{\nu_{p}(n)+1}\qquad\text{for every prime }p\mid n.

Necessity follows from the count above. Sufficiency requires more: terms divisible by different primes may need the same divisors as coprime partners. By Hall’s theorem [2], a coprime matching exists if and only if, for every subset X⊆𝒫X\subseteq\mathcal{P}, at least |X||X| divisors of nn are coprime to at least one element of XX. Theorem 1.1 shows that the counting bounds for individual primes already guarantee all these inequalities, even when the progression is not primitive.

The proof has two parts. We first construct a matrix whose entries are nonzero exactly when the corresponding integers are coprime. An invertible change of columns gives a Vandermonde matrix formed from distinct numbers. The original matrix therefore has a nonzero determinant, which proves that a coprime matching exists. This construction applies under explicit bounds on the exponents in the prime factorization of nn. For the remaining cases allowed by (1), we partition the progression into shorter progressions and combine matchings obtained from the same construction. The two special cases considered below use [1,τ⁡(n)][1,\tau(n)] or require a matching with every primitive arithmetic progression.

A classical related problem is a conjecture of D. J. Newman: if II is any interval of NN consecutive integers, then [1,N][1,N] admits a coprime matching with II. Pomerance and Selfridge proved this conjecture in 1980 [6]. Robertson and Small later replaced the interval by an arithmetic progression

S:={a+bt:t=0,1,…,N−1},a∈ℤ,b∈ℤ>0,S:=\{a+bt:t=0,1,\dots,N-1\},\qquad a\in\mathbb{Z},\quad b\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0},

and determined exactly when a coprime matching [1,N]→S[1,N]\to S exists [8]. In particular, such a matching exists whenever gcd⁡(a,b)=1\gcd(a,b)=1. Thus [1,N][1,N] admits a coprime matching with every primitive arithmetic progression of length NN. More recent work has studied the existence and number of coprime mappings and coprime permutations [4, 5, 9]; Bohman and Peng also connected coprime mappings between intervals with the lonely runner problem [1].

In 2022, Recamán called an integer nn matchable if D⁡(n)D(n) admits a coprime matching with [1,τ⁡(n)][1,\tau(n)] and asked whether matchable integers are more numerous than nonmatchable integers [7]. The ensuing discussion raised the problem of characterizing them. Among the comments on that question, König and the author conjectured that every integer not divisible by ppp^{p} for any prime pp should be matchable and that few integers outside this class should be matchable; McNew and Pomerance record these conjectures in [3]. König also asked whether every divisor of a matchable integer must itself be matchable. In the MathOverflow discussion [7], the author proposed the more precise criterion

(2) τ⁡(n/d)≤⌈(d−1)​τ​(n)d⌉for every ​d|rad⁡(n),d>1.\tau(n/d)\leq\left\lceil\frac{(d-1)\tau(n)}{d}\right\rceil\qquad\text{for every }d\mid\rad(n),\ d>1.

The condition is necessary, and the conjecture was verified computationally in the MathOverflow discussion for n≤105n\leq 10^{5}.

McNew and Pomerance subsequently initiated a systematic study of matchable numbers [3]. They call nn an MM-number if

pp∤nfor every prime ​p.p^{p}\nmid n\qquad\text{for every prime }p.

They proved that almost every MM-number is matchable, that every squarefree integer (one with no squared prime factor) is matchable, and that the integers belonging to exactly one of the classes of matchable integers and MM-numbers form a set of density zero. Here the asymptotic density of a set is the limiting proportion of integers in [1,X][1,X] that belong to it as X→∞X\to\infty; “almost every” allows a set of exceptions of density zero. Hence the matchable integers have asymptotic density

α:=∏p​prime(1−1pp)=0.72199023441955​….\alpha:=\prod_{p\ \mathrm{prime}}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{p}}\right)=0.72199023441955\ldots.

They explicitly endorsed the König–Alekseyev conjecture that every MM-number is matchable. They also observed that this would follow from König’s question about divisors, because every MM-number divides one of the explicitly matchable numbers MP:=∏q≤P,q​primeqq−1M_{P}:=\prod_{q\leq P,\ q\ \mathrm{prime}}q^{q-1}; they did not find a proof that matchability passes to divisors.

McNew and Pomerance also considered a stronger requirement. They use “coprime arithmetic progression” for what we call a primitive progression [3]. A positive integer nn is strongly matchable if D⁡(n)D(n) admits a coprime matching with every primitive arithmetic progression of length τ⁡(n)\tau(n). The Robertson–Small theorem gives such a matching from [1,τ⁡(n)][1,\tau(n)]; the question is whether D⁡(n)D(n) can replace this interval. McNew and Pomerance conjectured that nn is strongly matchable if and only if it is an MM-number [3, Conjecture 1].

We obtain the following characterization, proving this conjecture.

Theorem 1.2.

A positive integer is strongly matchable if and only if it is an MM-number.

The forward implication is [3, Proposition 4]. The Vandermonde construction gives the converse directly, before we prove the full progression criterion.

For matchings with [1,τ⁡(n)][1,\tau(n)], we obtain the following equivalent arithmetic criteria, including (2).

Theorem 1.3.

Let nn be a positive integer, put N:=τ⁡(n)N:=\tau(n), and let νp​(n)\nu_{p}(n) denote the exponent of pp in the prime factorization of nn. The following are equivalent.

  1. (i)

    nn is matchable.

  2. (ii)

    For every prime p|np\mid n,

    (3) ⌊Np⌋≤Nνp​(n)+1.\left\lfloor\frac{N}{p}\right\rfloor\leq\frac{N}{\nu_{p}(n)+1}.
  3. (iii)

    For every d|rad⁡(n)d\mid\rad(n), d>1d>1,

    (4) τ⁡(n/d)≤⌈(d−1)​Nd⌉.\tau(n/d)\leq\left\lceil\frac{(d-1)N}{d}\right\rceil.
  4. (iv)

    Either nn is an MM-number, or there is a unique prime pp with pp|np^{p}\mid n and

    (5) (νp​(n)+1−p)​τ​(npνp​(n))<p.\bigl(\nu_{p}(n)+1-p\bigr)\tau\!\left(\frac{n}{p^{\nu_{p}(n)}}\right)<p.

For 𝒫=[1,N]\mathcal{P}=[1,N], we have cp​(𝒫)=⌊N/p⌋c_{p}(\mathcal{P})=\lfloor N/p\rfloor, so (3) is precisely the counting condition in Theorem 1.1. When pp|np^{p}\mid n, McNew and Pomerance used the bound N/(νp​(n)+1)≤N/(p+1)N/(\nu_{p}(n)+1)\leq N/(p+1) to obtain a weaker necessary condition [3, Proposition 1]. The equivalence with part (iv) explicitly describes the matchable non-MM-numbers. It also answers König’s question about divisors of matchable integers.

Corollary 1.4.

Every divisor of a matchable integer is matchable.

Section 2 uses a Vandermonde determinant to establish a coprime matching, and Section 3 deduces Theorem 1.2. Section 4 proves Theorem 1.3 by partitioning [1,τ⁡(n)][1,\tau(n)] into shorter progressions. Section 5 adapts that partition to prove Theorem 1.1 and characterizes the common differences for which every primitive progression admits a matching. Section 6 explicitly describes the matchable non-MM-numbers, proves that matchability passes to divisors, and derives the density results.

2. A coprime matching from a Vandermonde determinant

We begin with the algebraic construction. The exponent bounds are needed only at primes not dividing the common difference, a fact we will use in Section 5.

Lemma 2.1 (Vandermonde matching lemma).

Let

m:=∏i=1rpiqi−1,m:=\prod_{i=1}^{r}p_{i}^{q_{i}-1},

where p1,…,prp_{1},\ldots,p_{r} are distinct primes and the qiq_{i} are positive integers, and put

Q:=τ⁡(m)=∏i=1rqi.Q:=\tau(m)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}q_{i}.

Let

𝒫:={a+bt:t=0,1,…,Q−1},a∈ℤ,b∈ℤ>0,gcd(a,b)=1.\mathcal{P}:=\{a+bt:t=0,1,\dots,Q-1\},\qquad a\in\mathbb{Z},\quad b\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0},\quad\gcd(a,b)=1.

If qi≤piq_{i}\leq p_{i} whenever pi∤bp_{i}\nmid b, then D⁡(m)D(m) admits a coprime matching with 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

Proof.

If r=0r=0, then m=Q=1m=Q=1, and the only divisor, 11, is coprime to the only term of the progression. Assume r≥1r\geq 1 and fix a progression 𝒫\mathcal{P} as in the statement. Write [r]:={1,2,…,r}[r]:=\{1,2,\dots,r\} and split the indices into

I0:={i∈[r]:pi∤b},I1:={i∈[r]:pi∣b}.I_{0}:=\{i\in[r]:p_{i}\nmid b\},\qquad I_{1}:=\{i\in[r]:p_{i}\mid b\}.

For each i∈I0i\in I_{0}, choose a complex number ζi\zeta_{i} with ζipi=1\zeta_{i}^{p_{i}}=1 and ζi≠1\zeta_{i}\neq 1. Since pip_{i} is prime, ζik=1\zeta_{i}^{k}=1 for an integer kk exactly when pi|kp_{i}\mid k. For i∈[r]i\in[r], define

yi​(t):={ζia+b​t−1,i∈I0,pit,i∈I1.y_{i}(t):=\begin{cases}\zeta_{i}^{a+bt}-1,&i\in I_{0},\\ p_{i}^{t},&i\in I_{1}.\end{cases}

We list the divisors of mm in increasing order whenever they index a matrix. Consider the Q×QQ\times Q matrix MM, with rows indexed by t=0,1,…,Q−1t=0,1,\dots,Q-1 and columns indexed by the divisors d|md\mid m, whose entries are

(6) Mt,d:=∏i=1ryi​(t)νpi​(d).M_{t,d}:=\prod_{i=1}^{r}y_{i}(t)^{\nu_{p_{i}}(d)}.

We use the convention 00=10^{0}=1 in (6).

For i∈I0i\in I_{0}, the choice of ζi\zeta_{i} gives

yi(t)=0⟺pi∣a+bt.y_{i}(t)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p_{i}\mid a+bt.

The matrix VV is a Vandermonde matrix, with determinant

detV=∏f,g|mf<g(λg−λf)≠0.\det V=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}f,g\mid m\\ f<g\end{subarray}}(\lambda_{g}-\lambda_{f})\neq 0.

detM=∑σsgn⁡(σ)​∏t=0Q−1Mt,σ⁡(t),\det M=\sum_{\sigma}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{t=0}^{Q-1}M_{t,\sigma(t)},

where σ\sigma ranges over bijections from the row indices to the divisors of mm. Since this sum is nonzero, at least one σ\sigma has ∏tMt,σ⁡(t)≠0\prod_{t}M_{t,\sigma(t)}\neq 0. By (7), gcd⁡(a+b​t,σ⁡(t))=1\gcd(a+bt,\sigma(t))=1 for every tt. The bijection therefore gives a coprime matching between 𝒫\mathcal{P} and D⁡(m)D(m). ∎

Remark 2.2.

The determinant expansion shows that a square matrix with nonzero determinant has a choice of nonzero entries containing exactly one entry from each row and each column. For the matrix in (6), these entries give coprime pairs by (7). The determinant formula is standard. The definition of MM in (6) makes its nonzero entries correspond exactly to coprime pairs and allows the expansion in (8) to give the factorization M=V​AM=VA, with VV a Vandermonde matrix and detA≠0\det A\neq 0.

3. Strongly matchable numbers

We now prove Theorem 1.2.

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

First suppose that nn is an MM-number. Write

n=∏i=1rpiνpi​(n),qi:=νpi​(n)+1.n=\prod_{i=1}^{r}p_{i}^{\nu_{p_{i}}(n)},\qquad q_{i}:=\nu_{p_{i}}(n)+1.

The MM-number condition is precisely qi≤piq_{i}\leq p_{i} for every ii. For every positive common difference, the hypotheses of Lemma 2.1 therefore hold with m=nm=n. The lemma gives a coprime matching of D⁡(n)D(n) with every primitive arithmetic progression of length τ⁡(n)\tau(n). Hence nn is strongly matchable.

For completeness, we include the short argument for the converse implication already proved in [3, Proposition 4]. Suppose that nn is not an MM-number. Then for some prime pp,

νp​(n)≥p.\nu_{p}(n)\geq p.

Put N:=τ⁡(n)N:=\tau(n) and consider an interval of NN consecutive positive integers beginning at a multiple of pp. It contains ⌈N/p⌉\lceil N/p\rceil multiples of pp. Each would have to be matched to a divisor of nn not divisible by pp, but there are only N/(νp​(n)+1)N/(\nu_{p}(n)+1) such divisors. Since

Nνp​(n)+1<Np≤⌈Np⌉,\frac{N}{\nu_{p}(n)+1}<\frac{N}{p}\leq\left\lceil\frac{N}{p}\right\rceil,

no coprime matching exists. This interval is a primitive arithmetic progression, and therefore nn is not strongly matchable. ∎

The theorem also gives the following density result, strengthening [3, Proposition 6].

Corollary 3.1.

The strongly matchable integers have asymptotic density

α=∏p(1−1pp)=0.72199023441955​….\alpha=\prod_{p}\left(1-\frac{1}{p^{p}}\right)=0.72199023441955\ldots.
Proof.

By Theorem 1.2, the strongly matchable integers are exactly the integers not divisible by ppp^{p} for any prime pp. For any fixed PP, the Chinese remainder theorem shows that the integers avoiding ppp^{p} for primes p≤Pp\leq P have density ∏p≤P(1−p−p)\prod_{p\leq P}(1-p^{-p}). For every positive integer XX, the proportion of integers in [1,X][1,X] divisible by ppp^{p} for at least one prime p>Pp>P is at most ∑p>Pp−p\sum_{p>P}p^{-p}. This bound tends to zero as P→∞P\to\infty, because ∑pp−p\sum_{p}p^{-p} converges. Taking P→∞P\to\infty gives the claimed product. ∎

4. Characterization of matchable integers

Let nn be a positive integer and put N:=τ⁡(n)N:=\tau(n). For each prime p|np\mid n, the number of divisors of nn not divisible by pp is

Nνp​(n)+1.\frac{N}{\nu_{p}(n)+1}.

This gives the basic necessary condition.

Lemma 4.1 (A necessary inequality for each prime).

If nn is matchable, then for every prime p|np\mid n,

(12) ⌊Np⌋≤Nνp​(n)+1.\left\lfloor\frac{N}{p}\right\rfloor\leq\frac{N}{\nu_{p}(n)+1}.
Proof.

There are ⌊N/p⌋\lfloor N/p\rfloor multiples of pp in [1,N][1,N]. Each of them must be matched to a divisor of nn not divisible by pp, and there are exactly N/(νp​(n)+1)N/(\nu_{p}(n)+1) such divisors. ∎

The next lemma shows how restrictive the inequalities (12) are.

Lemma 4.2 (At most one prime pp with pp|np^{p}\mid n).

Suppose (12) holds for every prime p|np\mid n. Then at most one prime p|np\mid n satisfies νp​(n)+1>p\nu_{p}(n)+1>p. If such a prime exists, put

δ:=νp​(n)+1−p,m:=npνp​(n).\delta:=\nu_{p}(n)+1-p,\qquad m:=\frac{n}{p^{\nu_{p}(n)}}.

Then mm is an MM-number and

(13) δ​τ​(m)<p.\delta\,\tau(m)<p.
Proof.

Fix p|np\mid n and put T:=N/(νp​(n)+1)T:=N/(\nu_{p}(n)+1). If νp​(n)+1>p\nu_{p}(n)+1>p, put δ:=νp​(n)+1−p≥1\delta:=\nu_{p}(n)+1-p\geq 1. Then

⌊Np⌋=⌊(p+δ)​Tp⌋=T+⌊δ​Tp⌋.\left\lfloor\frac{N}{p}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\frac{(p+\delta)T}{p}\right\rfloor=T+\left\lfloor\frac{\delta T}{p}\right\rfloor.

Thus (12) is equivalent, for this prime, to δ​T<p\delta T<p.

Suppose two distinct primes pp and ℓ\ell satisfy pp|np^{p}\mid n and ℓℓ|n\ell^{\ell}\mid n. Put Tp:=N/(νp​(n)+1)T_{p}:=N/(\nu_{p}(n)+1). Since the factor νℓ​(n)+1\nu_{\ell}(n)+1 occurs in TpT_{p},

Tp=(νℓ​(n)+1)​∏q|nq≠p,ℓ(νq​(n)+1)≥νℓ​(n)+1>ℓ.T_{p}=(\nu_{\ell}(n)+1)\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\mid n\\ q\neq p,\ell\end{subarray}}(\nu_{q}(n)+1)\geq\nu_{\ell}(n)+1>\ell.

Since νp​(n)+1−p≥1\nu_{p}(n)+1-p\geq 1, the inequality just obtained gives

p>(νp​(n)+1−p)​Tp≥Tp>ℓ.p>\bigl(\nu_{p}(n)+1-p\bigr)T_{p}\geq T_{p}>\ell.

Interchanging pp and ℓ\ell gives ℓ>p\ell>p, a contradiction. Hence at most one prime pp satisfies pp|np^{p}\mid n. If such a prime exists, then νq​(n)+1≤q\nu_{q}(n)+1\leq q for every prime q|mq\mid m, which says exactly that mm is an MM-number. For this pp, we have T=τ⁡(m)T=\tau(m) and δ=νp​(n)+1−p\delta=\nu_{p}(n)+1-p, so the inequality δ​T<p\delta T<p is precisely (13). ∎

We can now construct a matching whenever (12) holds for every prime divisor of nn.

Proposition 4.3 (Sufficiency of the counting inequalities).

If (12) holds for every prime p|np\mid n, then nn is matchable.

Proof.

If nn is an MM-number, it is strongly matchable by Theorem 1.2 and hence matchable.

m:=npνp​(n),δ:=νp​(n)+1−p,m:=\frac{n}{p^{\nu_{p}(n)}},\qquad\delta:=\nu_{p}(n)+1-p,

N:=τ⁡(n)=(p+δ)​T=p​T+δ​T,⌊Np⌋=T.N:=\tau(n)=(p+\delta)T=pT+\delta T,\qquad\left\lfloor\frac{N}{p}\right\rfloor=T.

p​T<N<p⁡(T+1),pT<N<p(T+1),

p⁡[1,T]={p,2​p,…,T​p}.p[1,T]=\{p,2p,\ldots,Tp\}.

Since mm is strongly matchable, choose a coprime matching ϕ0:D⁡(m)→[1,T]\phi_{0}:D(m)\to[1,T]. The divisors in D⁡(m)D(m) are exactly the divisors of nn not divisible by pp. Match them to these multiples by

(14) d⟼p​ϕ0​(d).d\longmapsto p\phi_{0}(d).

Indeed,

gcd⁡(d,p​ϕ0​(d))=1,\gcd\bigl(d,p\phi_{0}(d)\bigr)=1,

because p∤dp\nmid d and gcd⁡(d,ϕ0​(d))=1\gcd(d,\phi_{0}(d))=1.

We now partition the remaining integers in [1,N][1,N], which are not divisible by pp. Those in [1,p​T][1,pT] split into the following p−1p-1 pairwise disjoint arithmetic progressions:

(15) 𝒫r:={r,r+p,…,r+(T−1)​p},1≤r≤p−1.\mathcal{P}_{r}:=\{r,r+p,\ldots,r+(T-1)p\},\qquad 1\leq r\leq p-1.

Each 𝒫r\mathcal{P}_{r} has length TT and is primitive because gcd⁡(r,p)=1\gcd(r,p)=1. Next,

(p+δ)​T=p​T+δ​T<p​T+p=p⁡(T+1),(p+\delta)T=pT+\delta T<pT+p=p(T+1),

[p​T+1,(p+δ)​T][pT+1,(p+\delta)T]

(16) 𝒬s:={p​T+(s−1)​T+1,…,p​T+s​T},1≤s≤δ.\mathcal{Q}_{s}:=\{pT+(s-1)T+1,\ldots,pT+sT\},\qquad 1\leq s\leq\delta.

Each 𝒬s\mathcal{Q}_{s} is a primitive arithmetic progression of length TT (with common difference 11). Thus we have the disjoint union

(17) [1,N]=p⁡[1,T]​∪˙​⋃˙r=1p−1𝒫r​∪˙​⋃˙s=1δ𝒬s.[1,N]=p[1,T]\;\dot{\cup}\;\mathop{\dot{\bigcup}}_{r=1}^{p-1}\mathcal{P}_{r}\;\dot{\cup}\;\mathop{\dot{\bigcup}}_{s=1}^{\delta}\mathcal{Q}_{s}.

progressions. For e≥1e\geq 1, write peD(m):={ped:d∣m}p^{e}D(m):=\{p^{e}d:d\mid m\}. There is therefore one progression for each of the sets

p​D​(m),p2​D​(m),…,pνp​(n)​D​(m),pD(m),p^{2}D(m),\ldots,p^{\nu_{p}(n)}D(m),

List the progressions in the last two families of (17) as ℬ1,…,ℬνp​(n)\mathcal{B}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{B}_{\nu_{p}(n)}. For every 1≤e≤νp​(n)1\leq e\leq\nu_{p}(n), strong matchability of mm supplies a coprime bijection

ϕe:D⁡(m)⟶ℬe.\phi_{e}:D(m)\longrightarrow\mathcal{B}_{e}.

gcd⁡(pe​d,ϕe​(d))=1(d∈D⁡(m)).\gcd\bigl(p^{e}d,\phi_{e}(d)\bigr)=1\qquad(d\in D(m)).

Hence

We next relate the inequalities (12) to the condition originally conjectured in [7].

Lemma 4.4.

For a positive integer nn with N:=τ⁡(n)N:=\tau(n), the following are equivalent:

  1. (a)

    (12) holds for every prime p|np\mid n;

  2. (b)
    (18) τ⁡(n/d)≤⌈(d−1)​Nd⌉(d∣rad⁡(n),d>1).\tau(n/d)\leq\left\lceil\frac{(d-1)N}{d}\right\rceil\qquad(d\mid\rad(n),\ d>1).
Proof.

For a prime p|np\mid n,

τ⁡(n/p)=N−Nνp​(n)+1,\tau(n/p)=N-\frac{N}{\nu_{p}(n)+1},

while, because NN is an integer,

⌈(p−1)​Np⌉=N−⌊Np⌋.\left\lceil\frac{(p-1)N}{p}\right\rceil=N-\left\lfloor\frac{N}{p}\right\rfloor.

Hence the d=pd=p instance of (18) is exactly (12). Thus (b) implies (a).

Conversely, suppose (a), let d|rad⁡(n)d\mid\rad(n) with d>1d>1, and choose a prime p|dp\mid d. Since n/dn/d divides n/pn/p,

τ⁡(n/d)≤τ⁡(n/p).\tau(n/d)\leq\tau(n/p).

Using the prime case and p≤dp\leq d gives

τ⁡(n/d)\displaystyle\tau(n/d) ≤τ⁡(n/p)\displaystyle\leq\tau(n/p)
≤⌈(p−1)​Np⌉\displaystyle\leq\left\lceil\frac{(p-1)N}{p}\right\rceil
≤⌈(d−1)​Nd⌉,\displaystyle\leq\left\lceil\frac{(d-1)N}{d}\right\rceil,

which proves (b). ∎

The same argument applies to every divisor d>1d>1 of nn, without requiring dd to be squarefree. Thus the equivalent criterion may also be imposed for all d|nd\mid n, d>1d>1; the squarefree formulation in Theorem 1.3 retains the original conjecture.

Proof of Theorem 1.3.

The implication (i)⇒\Rightarrow(ii) is Lemma 4.1, while (ii)⇒\Rightarrow(i) is Proposition 4.3. Lemma 4.4 gives (ii)⇔\Leftrightarrow(iii).

If (ii) holds, Lemma 4.2 gives precisely the alternative in (iv). Conversely, if nn is an MM-number, then νp​(n)+1≤p\nu_{p}(n)+1\leq p for every p|np\mid n, and therefore

⌊Np⌋≤Np≤Nνp​(n)+1.\left\lfloor\frac{N}{p}\right\rfloor\leq\frac{N}{p}\leq\frac{N}{\nu_{p}(n)+1}.

If instead (iv) holds with a prime pp satisfying pp|np^{p}\mid n, put m:=n/pνp​(n)m:=n/p^{\nu_{p}(n)}. The uniqueness of pp implies that mm is an MM-number, so the preceding inequality holds for primes dividing mm. For pp, condition (3) is equivalent to (νp​(n)+1−p)​τ​(m)<p\bigl(\nu_{p}(n)+1-p\bigr)\tau(m)<p, which is exactly (5). Hence (iv)⇒\Rightarrow(ii), completing the equivalence. ∎

5. Matchings with prescribed arithmetic progressions

We now adapt the construction in Proposition 4.3 to a given arithmetic progression. Recall that Lemma 2.1 places no restriction on the exponent of a prime that divides the common difference.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Necessity follows because every term of the progression divisible by pp must be matched to one of the N/(νp​(n)+1)N/(\nu_{p}(n)+1) divisors not divisible by pp.

For sufficiency, assume (1) and put g:=gcd⁡(a,b)g:=\gcd(a,b). If a prime p|np\mid n divided gg, then cp​(𝒫)=Nc_{p}(\mathcal{P})=N, contradicting N/(νp​(n)+1)<NN/(\nu_{p}(n)+1)<N. Hence gcd⁡(g,n)=1\gcd(g,n)=1. Dividing every term by gg does not change which divisors of nn are coprime to it, or any of the counts cpc_{p}, and gives a primitive progression. We may therefore assume gcd⁡(a,b)=1\gcd(a,b)=1.

For every prime p|np\mid n with p∤bp\nmid b,

⌊Np⌋≤cp​(𝒫)≤Nνp​(n)+1.\left\lfloor\frac{N}{p}\right\rfloor\leq c_{p}(\mathcal{P})\leq\frac{N}{\nu_{p}(n)+1}.

As in the proof of Lemma 4.2, if such a prime also satisfies pp|np^{p}\mid n, put

Tp:=Nνp​(n)+1,δp:=νp​(n)+1−p.T_{p}:=\frac{N}{\nu_{p}(n)+1},\qquad\delta_{p}:=\nu_{p}(n)+1-p.

Then

Tp+⌊δp​Tpp⌋=⌊Np⌋≤Tp,T_{p}+\left\lfloor\frac{\delta_{p}T_{p}}{p}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\frac{N}{p}\right\rfloor\leq T_{p},

so δp​Tp<p\delta_{p}T_{p}<p. If two distinct primes p,ℓp,\ell satisfied these conditions, we would obtain

p>Tp≥νℓ​(n)+1>ℓ,p>T_{p}\geq\nu_{\ell}(n)+1>\ell,

and, by interchanging them, ℓ>p\ell>p, a contradiction. Thus at most one prime pp satisfies both pp|np^{p}\mid n and p∤bp\nmid b.

If no such prime exists, Lemma 2.1 applies directly with m=nm=n. Otherwise, let pp be the unique prime satisfying these two conditions, and put

m:=npνp​(n),T:=τ⁡(m),δ:=νp​(n)+1−p.m:=\frac{n}{p^{\nu_{p}(n)}},\qquad T:=\tau(m),\qquad\delta:=\nu_{p}(n)+1-p.

We have

δ​T<p,N=(p+δ)​T,\delta T<p,\qquad N=(p+\delta)T,

and every prime q|mq\mid m with q∤bq\nmid b satisfies νq​(m)+1≤q\nu_{q}(m)+1\leq q. No exponent bound is required at primes dividing bb.

We adapt the partition in Proposition 4.3. The first p​TpT terms of 𝒫\mathcal{P} split into the progressions

ℬr:={a+br+pbk:k=0,1,…,T−1},0≤r<p.\mathcal{B}_{r}:=\{a+br+pbk:k=0,1,\ldots,T-1\},\qquad 0\leq r<p.

Since p∤bp\nmid b, the integers a,a+b,…,a+(p−1)​ba,a+b,\ldots,a+(p-1)b have distinct remainders upon division by pp. Thus exactly one index r0r_{0} satisfies p|a+b​r0p\mid a+br_{0}. The progression ℬr0\mathcal{B}_{r_{0}} contains TT multiples of pp, and the other progressions contain none. The assumed bound cp​(𝒫)≤Tc_{p}(\mathcal{P})\leq T therefore implies that none of the final δ​T\delta T terms is divisible by pp.

The progression

p−1ℬr0={a+b​r0p+bk:k=0,1,…,T−1}p^{-1}\mathcal{B}_{r_{0}}=\left\{\frac{a+br_{0}}{p}+bk:k=0,1,\ldots,T-1\right\}

is primitive: any common divisor of its first term and bb would divide both aa and bb. By Lemma 2.1, choose a coprime matching from D⁡(m)D(m) to this progression. Multiplying each matched term by pp gives a coprime matching from D⁡(m)D(m) to ℬr0\mathcal{B}_{r_{0}}, since no divisor of mm is divisible by pp.

For r≠r0r\neq r_{0}, the progression ℬr\mathcal{B}_{r} is primitive with common difference p​bpb: its first term is coprime to bb and is not divisible by pp. Split the final δ​T\delta T terms into the following δ\delta progressions:

𝒞s:={a+b(pT+(s−1)T+k):k=0,1,…,T−1},1≤s≤δ.\mathcal{C}_{s}:=\{a+b(pT+(s-1)T+k):k=0,1,\ldots,T-1\},\qquad 1\leq s\leq\delta.

Each 𝒞s\mathcal{C}_{s} is primitive with common difference bb. Lemma 2.1 applies to D⁡(m)D(m) and each of these p−1+δ=νp​(n)p-1+\delta=\nu_{p}(n) remaining progressions. Indeed, since p∤mp\nmid m, the required exponent bounds for primes dividing mm are the same for common differences bb and p​bpb.

As in Proposition 4.3, pair these progressions, in any order, with the sets

p​D​(m),p2​D​(m),…,pνp​(n)​D​(m).pD(m),p^{2}D(m),\ldots,p^{\nu_{p}(n)}D(m).

For the progression paired with pe​D​(m)p^{e}D(m), replace each matched divisor dd by pe​dp^{e}d. Since none of the terms of these progressions is divisible by pp, every resulting pair remains coprime. Together with the matching from D⁡(m)D(m) to ℬr0\mathcal{B}_{r_{0}}, these matchings form the required bijection. ∎

Corollary 5.1 (Fixed common difference).

Let nn be a positive integer and fix b∈ℤ>0b\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}. Then D⁡(n)D(n) admits a coprime matching with every primitive arithmetic progression of length τ⁡(n)\tau(n) and common difference bb if and only if every prime pp for which pp|np^{p}\mid n divides bb.

Proof.

If every prime pp satisfying pp|np^{p}\mid n divides bb, Lemma 2.1 applies to every such progression. Conversely, suppose pp|np^{p}\mid n and p∤bp\nmid b, and put N:=τ⁡(n)N:=\tau(n). The primitive progression

{p+bt:t=0,1,…,N−1}\{p+bt:t=0,1,\ldots,N-1\}

contains ⌈N/p⌉\lceil N/p\rceil multiples of pp. Since

Nνp​(n)+1<Np≤⌈Np⌉,\frac{N}{\nu_{p}(n)+1}<\frac{N}{p}\leq\left\lceil\frac{N}{p}\right\rceil,

it violates the necessary condition in Theorem 1.1. ∎

6. Consequences

Solving the inequality in Theorem 1.3(iv) for νp​(n)\nu_{p}(n) gives the following explicit classification.

Corollary 6.1 (Explicit form).

A positive integer nn is matchable if and only if either it is an MM-number, or it has the form n=pe​mn=p^{e}m, where pp is prime, ee is an integer, p∤mp\nmid m, mm is an MM-number, and, with T:=τ⁡(m)T:=\tau(m),

T≤p−1,p≤e≤p−1+⌊p−1T⌋.T\leq p-1,\qquad p\leq e\leq p-1+\left\lfloor\frac{p-1}{T}\right\rfloor.

In the second case pp is the unique prime for which pp|np^{p}\mid n.

Proof.

For e≥pe\geq p, the condition in Theorem 1.3(iv) is equivalent to

(e+1−p)T<p⟺(e+1−p)T≤p−1⟺e≤p−1+⌊p−1T⌋.(e+1-p)T<p\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(e+1-p)T\leq p-1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad e\leq p-1+\left\lfloor\frac{p-1}{T}\right\rfloor.

Since e+1−p≥1e+1-p\geq 1, this also forces T≤p−1T\leq p-1. ∎

In particular, for every prime pp and integer e≥0e\geq 0,

pe is matchable⟺e≤2p−2.p^{e}\text{ is matchable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad e\leq 2p-2.

Indeed, exponents e<pe<p give MM-numbers, and for e≥pe\geq p the corollary applies with m=1m=1 and T=1T=1.

For example, the only matchable integer divisible by 222^{2} is 44. The matchable integers divisible by 333^{3} are 2727, 8181, and 27​q27q, where q≠3q\neq 3 is prime. The family 27​q27q was already noted in [3].

Proof of Corollary 1.4.

Let nn be matchable and let d|nd\mid n. If nn is an MM-number, then so is dd, and hence dd is matchable by Theorem 1.2.

Otherwise, Theorem 1.3(iv) gives a unique prime pp for which pp|np^{p}\mid n. Put m:=n/pνp​(n)m:=n/p^{\nu_{p}(n)} and δ:=νp​(n)+1−p\delta:=\nu_{p}(n)+1-p, and note that mm is an MM-number with δ​τ​(m)<p\delta\tau(m)<p. Put u:=d/pνp​(d)u:=d/p^{\nu_{p}(d)}; then u|mu\mid m. If νp​(d)<p\nu_{p}(d)<p, then dd is an MM-number and hence matchable by Theorem 1.2. If νp​(d)≥p\nu_{p}(d)\geq p, then

(νp​(d)+1−p)​τ​(u)≤(νp​(n)+1−p)​τ​(m)<p.\bigl(\nu_{p}(d)+1-p\bigr)\tau(u)\leq\bigl(\nu_{p}(n)+1-p\bigr)\tau(m)<p.

Theorem 1.3(iv) again shows that dd is matchable. ∎

This answers König’s question from the MathOverflow discussion: every divisor of a matchable integer is matchable. McNew and Pomerance observed that every MM-number divides one of

MP=∏q≤Pq​primeqq−1.M_{P}=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leq P\\ q\ \mathrm{prime}\end{subarray}}q^{q-1}.

Each MPM_{P} is matchable by the Chinese remainder theorem: match d|MPd\mid M_{P} to the unique t∈[1,τ⁡(MP)]t\in[1,\tau(M_{P})] satisfying t≡νq​(d)(modq)t\equiv\nu_{q}(d)\pmod{q} for every prime q≤Pq\leq P. These assignments are distinct, and q|dq\mid d implies q∤tq\nmid t, so the matched pairs are coprime. The result about divisors therefore implies that every MM-number is matchable. Our proof that matchability passes to divisors already uses Theorem 1.2, which gives strong matchability directly.

The explicit classification also recovers the density theorem of McNew and Pomerance [3]. Fix a prime pp and consider the matchable integers nn for which pp|np^{p}\mid n. Write n=pe​mn=p^{e}m with p∤mp\nmid m. Corollary 6.1 bounds both ee and τ⁡(m)\tau(m). If ω⁡(m)\omega(m) denotes the number of distinct prime factors of mm, then 2ω⁡(m)≤τ⁡(m)2^{\omega(m)}\leq\tau(m), so ω⁡(m)\omega(m) is bounded. Integers with a bounded number of distinct prime factors have density zero. Since only finitely many exponents of pp occur, the corresponding integers also form a set of density zero. For every positive integer XX, the proportion of integers in [1,X][1,X] divisible by ppp^{p} for some prime p>Pp>P is at most ∑p>Pp−p\sum_{p>P}p^{-p}. Combining this bound with the density-zero result for the finitely many primes p≤Pp\leq P, and then letting P→∞P\to\infty, shows that the matchable non-MM-numbers have density zero, in agreement with [3].

Remark 6.2.

In (2), the inequalities for composite dd follow from those for prime dd. The main step is proving that the inequalities for primes suffice to construct a coprime matching. The proof of Theorem 1.3 uses Theorem 1.2 to match D⁡(m)D(m) with the shorter progressions in the partition from Proposition 4.3. Lemma 4.2 shows that, when the counting inequalities hold, at most one prime pp can satisfy pp|np^{p}\mid n.
